subtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY PROPOSED BY THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Some time ago I directed a question to the Prime Minister as to whether Canada had been asked to sign the peace treaty with the United States which Secretary Kellogg has invited the other great powers to sign. May I to-day receive a reply to that question from the Prime Minister?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY PROPOSED BY THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Shortly after noon to-day
the minister of the United States called at my office and stated that he had been instructed to extend in the name of the government of the United States a cordial invitation to His Majesty's government in Canada to become one of the original parties to the treaty for the renunciation of war which is now under consideration. It was agreed that the text of the invitation should be made public in the United States, Canada and elsewhere in Friday morning's press. An answer has not yet been sent as there has not been an opportunity to have one prepared, but an answer to the communication will be sent very shortly.

Paragraph 25 says:
It was submitted that the tendency of the tariff, as affected by successive alterations, has been to lessen the protection upon the primary products of iron and steel and to encourage their importation from other countries as being the raw materials of iron and steel-fabricating and finishing industries in Canada.
In respect of this matter, we do not conceive it to be our duty to express any opinion, since the question is, as we were informed by the chairman of the tariff advisory board, who met us at our request, at the present moment under the consideration of that board. But we do regard it as our duty to record that the significance of this industry to the maritime provinces was forcibly brought home to us, not only in the manufacturing towns we visited in the maritimes but also throughout the agricultural districts of the martimes. We record this in order to emphasize the need for prompt action.
Then, with regard to bounties, paragraph 26 says:
It was pointed out to us that, at its inception, the Nova Scotia steel industry enjoyed national aid in the form of a bounty. This system of bounties prevailed for many years.
We were asked to recommend that a bounty should be again made avilable. In this connection we have thought it right to give consideration to a point which was emphasized in the course of thfe evidence, vi.-that a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty is given when imported coal is used for metallurgical purposes, and that this is tantamount to giving a bonus of that amount, since it means that the Dominion is yielding up money which otherwise under its general policy in regard to bituminous coal would accrue to it. While there are, no doubt, other angles from which this concession can

be regarded, it does in its operation have the effect of a bonus, and it is difficult to see how the same bonus can be denied to native coal.
Having regard to the bounty system previously applied, and to this aspect of the application of the drawback-
Then comes their recommendation:
-we recommend that a bonus should be given in respect of steel when Canadian coal is used in its manufacture, and that the bonus should be calculated on the basis of the present drawback for every ton of coal used in such manufacture.
Here we have a specific recommendation made by this commission, namely, that a bonus should be granted out of the federal treasury to the steel industry, calculated on the amount of coal that it takes to produce a ton of steel.	.
I read now from the brief supplied to the Duncan commission on which this recommendation was based:
The Steel And Coal Industries
The steady decadence of the steel and coal industries of Nova Scotia in the past four or five years has contributed far more than any other single factor to that general condition of business decline in which the recent movement for maritime rights finds economic sanction. These industries, when operating normally, support wage-earning communities comprising a quarter of the population of the province. Directly vital to six of the eighteen counties of Nova Scotia, they indirectly influence economic conditions in every part of the maritime provinces. The centres of population which have grown up around them have for many years constituted the best and most readily accessible market for the farmers and fishermen of eastern Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, for the fruit growers of the Annapolis valley, for the industries and mercantile houses of Halifax, Moncton and Saint John. Depression of the coal and Bteel industries must inevitably be reflected in disturbed economic conditions in the whole maritime region.
As has been said, tariff protection to Canadian industries is the approved and accepted national policy of the Dominion. It is not the purpose of this review of the situation either to defend or to criticize that policy. All that is relevant to the case is to point out that, while it is maintained, Nova Scotia industries may fairly claim to be entitled to share in its advantages to the same degree as the major industries of Quebec and Ontario. Protection, or free trade, or an exclusively revenue tariff may be advocated with some show of logic, hut surely no reasonable defence, no consideration based on equity or sound public policy, can be advanced in support of a system under which Nova Scotians are compelled to buy what they consume in a substantially protected home market, and to sell what they produce in a virtually unprotected one. Before suggesting a remedy for this anomalous condition, it is important to review the stages and retrace the steps by which it has been reached.
iMr. F. MacDonald.]
About thirty years ago the iron and steel industry was established in Nova Scotia upon a large scale and, because of its essential relation and vital importance to the coal industry, should be considered in conjunction with it. Like coal mining, the manufacture of steel at its inception was given assistance from the national treasury, both in the form of bounties on tonnage output and protective duties against. competing products entering Canada. The compelling reason for the establishment in eastern Canada of a large scale steel plant, was that here, and here alone in the whole Dominion, -were the conditions to be found which rendered possible the growth of such an industry, with its three roots in British soil. These three roots are Nova Scotia coal, Nova Scotia limestone, and Nova Scotia or Newfoundland iron ore.
The system of bounties to the steel industry was maintained from 1900 to 1911, when it was discontinued. The duties on steel and steel products, established in 1907, were, like the coal duties, specific amounts per ton. When these duties were imposed, steel prices were such that the industry then enjoyed a tariff protection ranging from 20 to 35 per cent on its various products. To-day those products have a market value of from twice to three times what it was in 1907, but there has been no upwmrd revision of the duties from then till now. The consequence is that the average duty on the output of the Nova Scotia steel industry is to-day less than 10 per cent, while many of its most important products have been placed on the free list in order to assist Ontario industries using steel as a basic material to meet American competition in central Canada.
As is pointed out in this brief, there has been a great decline in the steel industry of Nova Scotia; of that there can be no question. One of the greatest authorities probably in Oanada on the steel and coal question is Mr. F. W. Gray, and in Iron and Steel of Canada for January, 1928, there appears an article by him pointing out this fatal decline in the steel industry, and naming the various industries that have declined in production or gone out of business entirely. Let me quote from this article:
In 1913 there were in Canada twenty-two blastfurnaces, of which five had for some years been idle. In the autumn of 1927 there were in blast only four furnaces.
Following is the number and operating condition of Canadian blast-furnaces in 1913-as given by the director of the Mines branch at Ottawa-and the present conditions, as nearly as can be ascertained, viz.-
Dominion Iron & Steel Company, Sydney, Cape Breton. Six completed furnaces, two operated throughout 1913, four for 344, 334, 222 and 140 days, respectively. Condition at end of October, 1927, was one furnace in operation, and prospect of second furnace being blown in during November.
Nova Scotia Steel & Coal Co. Ltd. In 1913, one furnace at Sydney Mines, Cape Breton, operated 365 days. An additional stack was erected in 1918, but was never blown in. Both furnaces have been continuously idle since some time in 1920.

Steel Industry~Mr. MacDonald (C.B.)
Londonderry Iron & Mining Company, Londonderry, Nova Scotia. In 1913, one furnace, idle throughout that year, and since abandoned.
Canada Iron Corporation Ltd. Two small furnaces at Drummondville. Que., and one at Radnor Forges, Que., all idle throughout 1913. Two furnaces at Midland, Ont., operated for 226 and 172 days respectively during 1913. One of the Midland furnaces was in 1917 sold to the Algoma Steel Corporation, and was re-erected at Sault Ste. Marie. In 1927, all the smaller furnaces have been continuously idle since 1913 and are therefore abandoned. The single stack remaining at Midland, Ont., has been idle for yea rs.
Standard Iron Company of Canada, Dese-ronto, Ont. One furnace at Deseronto, operated for 220 days during 1913, and one furnace at Parry Sound, operated 92 days in 1913. In 1927 these furnaces stand in an abandoned condition, having been idle for years.
The Steel Company of Canada, Ltd., Hamilton, Ont. In 1913 two furnaces operated, one for 259 days and the other for 309 days. In 1927 these blast furnaces remain without addition to producing capacity, and one furnace only was in operation in October.
The Canadian Furnace Co., Ltd., Port Col-borne, Ont. One furnace, operated 95 days. This furnace has been idle since November, 1924.
Algoma Steel Company, Ltd., Sault Ste. Marie, Ont. Three furnaces operated for 361, 365 and 322 days respectively in 1913. In 1927 this company has four furnaces, including the one moved from Midland in 1917. One furnace only was in operation in October, 1927.
Atikokan Iron Company, Ltd., Port Arthur, Ont. One furnace of 100 tons capacity idle since 1911, and now presumably abandoned.
That tells the story of the decline of the steel-making industry in Canada during the last few years. What causes have contributed to this decline? As to this, we are also in possession of the opinion of a leading authority, Mr. Rosts H. McMaster, the president of T.he Steel Company of Canada. In the May issue of Industrial Canada, he writes:
Our adopted form of federal taxation derives the largest share of its proceeds from organized business, so it seems abundantly evident that industry, in manufacturing and other lines, should be preserved in a healthy state.
It should be equally recognized that, when products manufactured in Canada yield almost twenty-five cents in taxes for every dollar of added value produced, it is a poor bargain for this country to admit commodities similar to those produced at home without payment of any contribution to our federal or other exchequers.
A contrary policy, however, has been followed, as an examination of our tariff reveals that there are 55 items which admit steel and iron of various descriptions duty free, or provide a drawback of substantially the entire duty when intended for particular purposes.
I want to put on record the items in the customs tariff relating to the duties on iron and steel. Item 1002 reads:
56103-206J
Rolled iron, rolled steel and pig iron: when used in the manufacture of mowing machines, reapers, harvesters, binders and attachments for binders.
Item 1005 reads:
Steel under one-half inch in diameter or under one-half inch square: when used in the manufacture of locks and knobs.
I would refer the house to the foregoing items and also to items 1006, 1007, 1009, 1015, 1019, 1021, 1026, 1028, 1036, 1045, 1046. 1047, 1048 and 1049. Anyone who cares to look up these items will find out for himself that the steel industry of Nova Scotia has been discriminated against.
In addition to its function of producing revenue, the customs tariff is expected to give equal protection or assistance to working people in the matter of wages and continuity of employment. It is submitted that a ton of steel produced in Nova Scotia, at a cost of $40, represents about twice as much directly in Canadian labour and, indirectly in Canadian material produced by Canadian labour, as a ton of similar steel produced elsewhere in Canada, So much for the decline of this industry, and so much for the cause of it.
For some years the industry fought a losing fight in Nova Scotia and the effect was not confined to the industry itself; it extended particularly to the great coal mining industry with which it is allied. But it was felt also, as is pointed out in one of the articles from which I have quoted, throughout all the industries and all the commerce of eastern Canada, The maritime provinces, as had been frequently stated, had been going behind and for many years had been losing their population. The people, young and old', had been leaving the country; farms were being abandoned; banks were going out of business; and their trust companies tad financial institutions were gradually leaving them and going to the larger centres. Then last, but not least, came the threatened collapse of their great industry'. It was this prospect that caused many thoughtful people throughout the maritime provinces to get together some few years ago to look into the reasons for this decline with a view to suggesting the remedy to be applied. Out of this welter came the movement which afterwards was known as " maritime rights", a movement which at its inception was more or less an object of ridicule. Many people appeared to affect a sort of laughing attitude when considering this question of maiitime rights, and the poor political prophets did not see in that movement a cloud which, while no larger than a man's
3252	COMMONS
Steel Industry-Mr. MacDonald (C.B.)
hand when it first appeared on the political horizon, gradually grew in extent. They did not then recognize it. In 1921 the Liberals swept the province of Nova Scotia from end to end; not a solitary Conservative was elected to this house from that province. In the local election an almost similar result obtained, for in a house of forty-three members there were only three Conservatives. Surely, they thought, under such circumstances they could afford to ignore this movement, which some of their members designated pure propaganda. And they tried to ascribe it to the' desperate efforts of some Tories to rehabilitate themselves in political life. But it went a little deeper than that. It was not a political movement at all at its inception, nor did it become so later. But the first indication, or the first sign that should have been an indication, of the growth of this movement came in 1923 when the solid block from Nova Scotia was broken by the election of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Black). Then followed the local elections in 1925. Here, of course, they felt on very firm ground. They had been in power in Nova Scotia for such a length of time that the memory of tnan runneth not to the contrary. For over forty years the Liberals had controlled the destinies of that province, and they got so at last that they could not distinguish between their own money and the people's-with somewhat disastrous results to some of them after the Conservatives came in. However, they went into the election, of 1925 with banners flying and with a very confident air of victory. But they came back with the figures reversed:	there were forty Conservatives
elected and three Liberals. That surely should have been some indication that the movement was gaining ground. Followed elections in the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. It should, I say, have been a lesson to those people who were paying no attention at all to this demand of the maritime provinces for recognition of their rights. But they continued to ignore the growth of that movement, and even the right hon. the Prime Minister himself (Mr. Mackenzie King), when touring the province in 1925, affected a sort of jocular attitude and asked, " What are these maritime rights?" The right hon. gentleman got his answer in the election that fallowed, because of that solid bloc, elected to support him in 1921 only two re' turned as a result of the 1925 conflict. But whatever may be said of the right hon. gentleman, no one can discount his resourcefulness; and at the opening of parliament in 1926 he inserted in the speech from the throne the 
following paragraph which he thought would certainly have some effect in placating those who came from the maritime provinces:
With a view to affording such remedies as may appear to be practical and appropriate, the government also propose to appoint a royal commission to inquire fully into the claims that the rights of the maritime provinces in regard to the operation of the Intercolonial railway have not been observed, and that in regard to transportation, immigration, and other economic factors these provinces have suffered prejudi-cally, in their position under confederation.
That idea did not commend itself to members from the maritime provinces; the history of previous investigations by commissions of this kind showed them only too well the danger which might result if that course were followed. We did oppose the appointment of any commission. In that we may have been wrong; I am not going to say now that we were not wrong, as it has turned out, but we thought at the time that before a committee of this house we could bring all the evidence of the conditions in the maritime provinces which would justify the house in believing there was something wrong with economic conditions in that part of Canada, and we thought we could suggest remedies for those conditions. The house will remember that during the session of 1926 all those who were opposed to the idea of maritime rights rose in their places and said how sympathetic they were and how much they desired to help us if only someone would tell them what maritime rights were. We thought we could tell them if we had a committee of the house, but the government thought otherwise and appointed Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, Professor Macmillan and Judge Wallace as a commission.
As soon as that commission was appointed our whole attitude changed; we loyally accepted the commission and appeared before it. Our three local governments prepared briefs in which they submitted their case to the commission; those gentlemen went into every aspect of the situation and followed up every clue which they thought might be of benefit. Let me here refer to a remark made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) in discussing the findings of this commission. He said this was an ex-parte commission, and I want to correct that impression; it was not an ex-parte commission in any sense of the term. The commission did not confine itself to the evidence laid before it by the interested parties; it went all over the country calling witnesses and seeking in every manner to obtain information which would permit of an honest and just

Steel Industry-Mr. MacDonald (C.B.)
finding. It concluded its work and filed its report with the government in September of 1926.
That report came as a great surprise to many people, who had been led to believe that there was nothing in this cry of maritime rights, that it was nothing more or less than the groans of a number of disgruntled' politicians who were looking for office. These people found from the report that there was something very wrong with conditions in the maritime provinces, so we looked with considerable anxiety to the attitude the government would take in connection with the report. On March 18, 1927, the Prime Minister made his statement with regard to maritime claims and the Duncan report. I do not propose to read it all but I will quote that paragraph which is germane to the point now under discussion. He said:
The recommendation of the commission that the tariff advisory board should be asked to give immediate consideration to the customs tariff in its relation to coal, anthracite and coke has been met. The matter is now before the tariff advisory board. It would appear desirable at this point to recall that at the session of 1925, as a means of assisting coal production in the mardtimes, the customs duty on slack coal was raised from 13 cents to 50 cents. The question of protection on the primary products of iron and steel was, as stated in the report, under the consideration of the tariff advisory board at the time of the commission's investigation. Owing to the existing uncertainty of conditions surrounding the iron and steel industry in the mardtimes. the government does not feel in a position to make at present any pronouncement with respect to the commission's recommendation of a renewal of the system of granting bounties with respect to steel when Canadian coal is used in its manufacture.
Then the Prime Minister concluded his statement in the following words:
In concluding this statement, may I say that the government hopes that, by accepting as we have, the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Maritime Claims, virtually in their entirety, parliament and the country will recognize in the attitude of the government a wish to remove this great question as largely as possible from the arena of sectional discord and party strife, and a desire to give to our Dominion in the sixtieth anniversary of its founding, a renewed expression of the spirit which animated the fathers of confederation in their efforts to construct out of British North America a federal union under a system of government devised "to protect the diversified interests of the several provinces and secure efficiency, harmony and permanency in the working of the union."
That eloquent peroration on the part of the Prime Minister appealed to many of us; we thought the government had dealt fairly generously with us. I am free to confess, however, that there was a difference of opinion
among the maritimers on that point; some of us believed that we should give the government credit for what they had done, and also make it clear to them that they were simply carrying out an instalment of the recommendations rather than virtually complying with all of them. Some others, and probably time has proved the wisdom of their prophecy, felt that the government did not intend to implement the Duncan report in its entirety, and they thought it just as well to say so frankly at the time. That difference of opinion continued until the fall of 1927, when the genial and gentlemanly Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) appeared before a meeting at St. John and announced what we considered at the time and what we still consider to be the policy of the government. There he said that when the budget came down there would be good news for the people of the maritime provinces, that everybody would be glad, that the government had already implemented the Duncan report with the exception of the recommendations touching the Valley railways and the steel bounties, and now when the budget came down the people of the maritime provinces would see that this great paternal government here had dealt with these matters in such a way that the people of the maritimes would be glad. I am happy to see that the Postmaster General has just taken his seat. This matter has been brought to the attention of the house several times and his remarks have been quoted here. When the budget debate took place we expected him to make a clear-cut pronouncement as to what he meant at that time, when he gave that news to the people of the maritime provinces. We do hope that he was not speaking entirely without authority, and that he had something up his sleeve. He hope that the hon. gentleman is going to carry out his promises to the maritime provinces before this session closes.
Such is the position at the present time. Those of us who put confidence in the government's promises one year ago were led to expect that when the time came they would fulfil all the recommendations, not only virtually but substantially in their entirety. Here is one clearcut reoomendation: a bounty of 50 cents a ton on native mined coal, used in the production of iron and steel.
What is the attitude of the government? I presume we can take that attitude to be defined by our representative in the cabinet, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). On March 5, when the minister spoke on the budget, regarding this question of the Duncan report, he said:
3254	COMMONS
Steel Industry-Mr. MacDonald (C.B.)
But there still remain certain things to be done. It seems to me that it is in the interest of this industry and in the interest of the Dominion that-first, there should be unity between the coal and steel businesses. Secondly, there should be a shrinkage of the capital so that the industry will have an opportunity of earning a dividend on some reasonable investment. Thirdly, the unwieldy organization should be simplified. It now consists of some fourteen companies. Fourthly, there ought to be co-operation by the provincial and municipal authorities in the work of building up this great industry. With the litigation ended and these conditions met, the way will be open for serious consideration by the federal government of the presentation of the real and legitimate needs of the industry.
That is very far from implementing the Dimoan report with regard to the bounty on steel. The Duncan report calls for a bounty, it does not call for any unity of industry, because they are all united. It does not call for any simplification, because they are all one concern now. The co-operation that the minister asks for has already been accomplished. The city has given the concern a five-year lease at a nominal rental and all these conditions were fulfilled before the minister made his speech. But if they were never fulfilled, they are conditions that should never be imposed on this industry. The Duncan commission made certain specific recommendations, and they should be carried out, or the government will have to take the responsibility.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), speaking on April 16, 1928, referring to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), said:
All he has done recently has been to tell the people of Canada who sometimes complain that this government have not reduced duties to the extent expected-and I am talking more particularly of the people who support this government

that by our trade agreements with other countries we have materially reduced the customs duties on goods coming into this country. I am not backing away from that point. We have materially reduced the duties. When our friends quote the general tariff as the measure of protection, they are all wrong. The duties on most of the items imported are based on the British preference or on the trade agreements which we have made with other countries, and we have exposed our own industries- I admit it frankly-to keen competition with other countries throughout the world. That is the policy of the government and the policy of the Canadian people as determined at the polls. Just as soon as they decide for a higher tariff they will elect by hon. friends opposite :o office.
The customs returns for March, 1928, show that over $260,000,000 worth of iron and steel and their products were imported into the Dominion. These goods should have been manufactured here and every dollar of that
fMr. F. MacDonald.]
money kept in the country. I received a telegram which I read in the house before showing the feelings of the men employed in this great industry. This telegram, dated February 19, 1927, is addressed to me and I will read it again:
Elected representatives of three thousand steel workers in conference this date urge that immediate action be taken by your government to adopt the recommendations of the Duncan Royal Commission on Maritime Rights.
J. J. Holmes,
Secretary
Genera] Works Committee, Dominion Iron and Steel Co. Ltd.
Our case for remedial legislation with respect to the steel industry is not based on a demand for any particular fiscal policy, but on a claim for equal treatment with other important Canadian industries under any general federal policy approved by parliament. It is repugnant to the federal idea that any province should be compelled to buy in a protected market and sell in an unprotected one. Steel and ooal represent to the people of Nova Scotia what the vast chain of industries established throughout Ontario and Quebec mean to the people of central Canada. This industry should be encouraged and conserved for the following reasons:
1.	All its raw materials are derived from British sources.
2.	It is essential to winter employment in the coal fields of Nova Scotia.
3.	Linked up with the coal industry as it is, it is by far the most important enterprise, in an economic sense, in the maritime provinces, where all classes and occupation are directly concerned in its prosperity.
4.	There can be no assured, independent industrial future for Canada., unless the basic products of iron and steel, which constitute the raw materials for so large a range of other industries, can be furnished from Canadian sources. No single case can be cited of a great manufacturing country which is dependent for its supplies of iron. Steel and ooal on the resources of its foreign industrial rivals.
5.	It would be difficult bo over-estimate the future economic value to Canada of a well established iron and steel industry, deriving its raw materials from native sources, and oapaible of expansion from time bo time to meet the requirements of the home market. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1928, upwards of $260,000,000 worth of iron and steel and their products were imported into the Dominion. Canada is to-day the best outside market the United States has for such products, and it is a market which is inereas-

Steel Industry-Mr. Cantley
ing in capacity year after year. That the Canadian steel industry should be allowed to languish and decline under such circumstances; that Canadian plants should slow down their production below 50 per cent of their capacity at the .very peak of the home market demand, is surely notice to the whole country of the urgent need of some revision of the public policy, under which such conditions are possible.
In view of these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Cantley, the amendment now in your hands.

Mr. Speaker, a year ago or a little more I called the attention of the house to this same subject. I did so at that time with the full concurrence and support of my then chief, the then leader of the Conservative party on this side of the house. As the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) has stated; some of my friends differed with me in regard to the wisdom of acting as I did. Some of them then had a little more faith in the government than I then had; as a matter of fact I had very little then and I have very little still.
In dealing with the matter a year ago I referred to the various provisions of the report of the Duncan commission and I stated that they might be reduced to eighteen. There has been some little change in regard to some of these as they have to a certain extent been further implemented than they were a year ago, but in the main there is very little difference. The twenty per cent freight reduction in part, has been applied. I say in part because it has been applied only in part. What important feature of the twenty per cent freight reduction has not been implemented? I refer to the international traffic, traffic originating in Canada and destined for points in the United States. So far as that is concerned we are not getting what the Duncan commission suggested we should get, with the result that a large portion of the freight originating in Price Edward Island and the great majority in value and tonnage of the freight originating in New Brunswick and to some extent in Nova Scotia are denied the twenty per cent reduction. I am referring to potatoes and lumber. Another recommendation of the Duncan commission was the enlargement of the scope and power of the railway commission. That has not been implemented. The recommendation in regard to the horizontal war freight increases has not been implemented.
I now come to the Prince Edward Island car ferry and I will refer to what the commission stated in regard to that; they dealt at considerable length with and made some recommendations in regard to the question of transportation for Prince Edward Island Some of those recommendations have been carried out and some have not. A portion of the island railway is still a narrow gauge road and on that portion it is impossible to-day to operate the modem refrigerator or frost-proof railway cars, so that the people in that section of the country are not able during the winter months to take advantage of railway facilities as are their brethren in other portions of the island. That portion of the Duncan commission's report has not been implemented. The commission dealt at length with the question of the car ferry. They said that they had taken the matter up with the railway people and that it was admitted that the boat service was unsatisfactory. They went on to state:
The railway administration admitted that there was need for supplemental provision being made in the form either of a second ferry boat or a special freight boat. We recommend that the matter be gone into from the point of view of placing at the disposal of the island such satisfactory means of communication as will ensure as regular and complete a service as can reasonably be made. We further recommend that, so far as the ferry boat service is concerned, it should not be run as part of the railway operations-
And so on. That last recommendation is a matter in which I am not particularly interested, but much can be said in regard to the car ferry. I find that some time ago the matter was taken up and a memorial was presented to the Railway department by the producers, merchants and exporters of the province of Prince Edward Island. Among other requests which they made was one that there should at once be built and put upon the connecting route a powerful, icebreaking car-ferry steamer equal in strength, power and capacity to the steamer Prince Edward Island now used as the connecting link, thereby affording better facilities and minimizing the risk of a dislocation of traffic by accidents of navigation. That was some time ago. Then I find that the Prince Edward Island Associated Boards of Trade in August, 1927, went on record and passed a resolution in regard to the need of a second car ferry on the Borden-Cape Tormentine route as recognized by the maritime royal commission.
I find that another resolution was passed on January 18, last, as follows:
Resolved that the representatives of this county, in the House of Commons, and also the representatives of Prince and Kings counties, and the four Prince Edward Island senators be
Steel Industry-Mr. Cantley

urged to exert every effort to impress upon the government and parliament of Canada the necessity and urgency that provision be made for the immediate construction of a new steamer for the Prince Edward Island car ferry service
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Sinclair) was present and agreed with the sentiments expressed in the resolution. Resolutions asking for a second car-ferry steamer have been passed by boards of trade on numerous occasions and sent to Ottawa. In September, 1920, the Maritime board of trade at its annual meeting in Amherst unanimously passed a resolution asking that another car-ferry steamer be provided.
I have under my hand a letter received from a gentleman who is a native of Prince Edward Island, a citizen of Charlottetown, with interests in other sections of the island and intimately connected with business and farming interests throughout the island, a man whose word would be accepted by anybody in the island who knows him. He writes as follows:
Several prominent citizens here have suggested a public meeting to urge on the government the fulfilment of the Duncan report for the island. They seem of the opinion it is better to wait until the estimates are brought down. Then we shall know if the government is serious about a second ferry boat. The Island Farmers' Association-a very large and influential organization here-passed strong resolutions recently requesting, even demanding better transportation. The Associated Boards of Trade have left no stone unterned.
Then he goes on and says further:
Here is an illustration of our need: You know that potatoes are our great commodity. Within the last year or two winter marketing of them has greatly increased because the southern traders who supply the American farmers with our seed stock do not want to keep them in warehouses there. They want them delivered only as the southern farmers need them. Go any day when the thermometer registers 20 or over, one may see hundreds of teams on our country roads. But the great difficulty is a famine for cars. The ferry cannot bring in empties-refrigerators-fast enough nor export loaded ears fast enough. At the present time the shippers are three hundred cars short, and they are half crazy to get their supply away for they fear a slump in prices and some of them would be ruined. Then the southeast section of the island which is served by a narrow gauge line are still -worse off. There are no frost proof cars for narrow gauge tracks. They have to ship in ordinary cars and many carloads have been ruined by freezing. Those farmers are moreover discriminated against by the expense of an extra handling of their shipments into broad gauge ears. And yet, John E. Sinclair will say the farmers are satisfied.
I have a further letter, dated May 5, which deals with the same subject, but I shall not burden the house with that, though it is even stronger than the other one.
[Mr. Cariiley.l
I have also a resolution which was passed unanimously by the government of Prince Edward Island on the 26th of April last, as follows:
Whereas in this province the production of potatoes for both seed and table stock is becoming annually of greater volume and value;
And whereas there is evidence that the acreage planted with potatoes in 1928 will exceed by 20 per cent the acreage of 1927;
And whereas the transportation facilities as provided were not sufficient to move the 1927 crop of potatoes at a time when they should be marketed.
Then follow a number of other "whereas" clauses, and the resolution concludes:
Resolved that this legislature now assembled hereby strongly urge the federal authorities to take immediate action for the construction of a new and suitable car ferry to be placed on the Borden-Tormentine route at the earliest possible date.
Moved by Horace Wright and P. A. Scully.
I am sorry the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) is not in his place, because I would like to get some information from him in regard to the position and the condition of the three ferry boats-the Prince Edward, and the Scotia No. 1 and the Scotia No. 2. I think the house is now familiar with the situation so far as the ferry service between Tormentine and the island is concerned, and the necessity for that service. I will now refer to the character of the steam ferry boats operated by the railway department. The steamer Prince Edward Island is a boat thirteen years old. She is off that route just now, and will be off it for a month. She has been off the route every year for about the same length of time, due to the fact that she has to dry dock at Halifax and pass her annual survey. It will be within the knowledge of all my friends in the house who are familiar with shipping that all steel vessels, on obtaining the age of ten. years, have to pass what is known as their No. 3 survey, and after that undergo an annual survey and overhaul. Some of these surveys are more exacting and take a longer time than others, and in the case of a boat as old as the Prince Edward Island about one month is required to complete the inspection and overhaul. This boat is one of very considerable power. She has three sets of triple engines, two sets aft, and one set forward. She has considerable water ballast, although not as much as she should have in view of the conditions under which she has to work, the total water ballast being 689 tons. This vessel was built under special survey at Lloyd's, so far as her machinery and boilers were concerned, but so far as I can find from Lloyd's register, and I

Steel Industry-Mr. Cantley
have looked up the last volume available, which is that for the present year, nothing has been done to maintain this vessel's classification. There is no indication on the book that her classification is being maintained. I do not say that it is not; I do not know whether it is or not, but there is no information on Lloyd's register that such is the case.
Now I want to contrast the treatment given this boat, and contrast her record in Lloyd's with the record of the three boats on the Pacific coast-the Prince George, the Prince John and the Prince Rupert, which were built for and operated in connection w;ith the Grand Trunk Pacific, now the Canadian National. The record shows that the boilers of all these three boats were inspected, one in January, one in February, and one in March of last year, 1927, but there is no such record so far as the Prince Edward Island is concerned. While this boat is away from the Prince IJdward Island service, her place is taken by one of the two boats which are on station at Mulgrave to maintain the traffic between the mainland and the island of Cape Breton. I do not know which of these boats is to-day relieving the Prince Edward. I have not been able to get that information;
I have asked for it, but have not been supplied with it. The Scotia I is the older boat of the two; she is twenty-seven years old. She was built at Newcastle by Armstrong, Whitworth and Company. This boat has no classification in Lloyd's. The other boat was built in 1915, the same year as the Prince Edward Island; she is thirteen years old. She is a considerably larger boat than the Scotia No. 1, which I think is the boat relieving the Prince Edward Island at the present time, but her power is less than one-half that of the Prince Edward Island while the oldest Scotia, which is twenty-seven years old, has about one-quarter the power of the Prince Edward Island. One or other of these boats is now attempting to do what the Prince Edward Island, a much larger and much more powerful boat, cannot do, that is to give an efficient service to the province of Prince Edward Island.
The question was asked the Minister of Railways at a meeting of the special committee on railways and shipping, as to whether any arrangements had been made for building this year an additional boat for this service, and I was told by the president of the road, and also I think by the Minister of Railways, whom I now see coming into the chamber, that no provision was being made this year in that respect, and that no amount would be provided in the estimates for this
service. Now that the Minister of Railways has come into the chamber I would ask him, will any provision be made in the railway estimates this year for a new island ferry boat to supplement the work that is being done by the Prince Edward?

Perhaps my hon. friend
would give me a chance to get into supply, and then we can deal with such matters as are in the estimates.

Pardon me, but that is
not a straight answer. I will give you all the time you want to answer my question now.

You are preventing me
from answering it.

I beg your pardon; I
am waiting for an answer now.

I should be pleased to
deal with the railway estimates when my hon. friend permits me to get them before the house, but if it will help him at all, I can assure him that the people of Prince Edward Island are likely to be pleased with the estimates of my department relating to that province.
I am glad to know that. I asked a similar question at a meeting of the railways and shipping committee, and received the answer that nothing was going to be done this year in regard to that matter.
From whom?

From yourself, I think,
and also from the president of the road. Am I reporting correctly what occurred at that time?
I do not think so.
Will the minister be good enough to tell me what answer was given me?

I shall be very glad
to look it up in the proceedings of the committee.

I have given the answer
that was given to me, and I think it is correct.

quote from the proceedings of the committee in relation to that matter, then neither of us will have to rely on our memory.

Perhaps the house would like to have some idea of how the Island people themselves
Steel Industry-Mr. Cantley

regard the matter. I have here a copy of the Charlottetown Guardian of February 11, 1928, in which reference is made to the Canadian Press report from Ottawa of February 8, and it credits the Postmaster General with the following:
Mr. Veniot declared that the recommendations of the Duncan report had been fully implemented with respect to Prince Edward Island, and this fact had already been pointed out by one of the members from that province.
The article continues:
Hon. Mr. Yeniot is evidently acting on the previous statement and assurance given in the house by Hon. John E. Sinclair, that he was entirely satisfied with the way the government had carried out the Duncan report recommendations in so far as it was possible to do.
Such an admission as this sent broadcast throughout the Dominion leaves a false impression and will do the ease of Prince Edward Island incalculable injury. As an instance, look at the interpretation the Hon. Mr. Veniot has placed on Mr. Sinclair's statement when he announces "that the recommendations of the Duncan report had been fully implemented with respect to Prince Edward Island."
Is Mr. Sinclair advancing the interests of Prince Edward Island by permitting such unjustifiable statements to be sent broadcast absolutely contrary to the facts? Will any prominent shipper, business man, or farmer in this province endorse Mr. Sinclair's statement ?
I will not detain the house by reading the remainder of the article. The matter is again taken up on March 11, when reference is made to the second car ferry and information requested. In the main it follows along the same lines as the preceding article from which I have quoted. I find a third article in which the members for Prince Edward Island on the government side are referred to as " rubber stamps." I will not weary the house by quoting it. It is in short a bitter complaint in regard to the way in which the island has been treated with respect to a second car ferry and the further extension of the standard gauge to the island railway.
Now, I cannot get the minister even to suggest that this year the department will provide an additional boat. Perhaps he will remember at this stage that two additional ferries are proposed for lake Michigan in connection with the western Grand Trunk division of the Canadian National Railways. Perhaps he will inform the house if those boats will be built this year, and if he thinks the interests of our American friends which would be served by those boats are more important than the interests of the people of Prince 'Edward Island.
One of the observations made by the Duncan commission is:

The outstanding fact, it seems to us, is that the maritime provinces have not prospered and developed, either in population, or in commercial, industrial and rural enterprise, as fully as other portions of Canada.
I propose to give lion, members some figures in regard to the increase in the population of the maritime provinces since confederation. I am going to contrast, in this respect, the three maritime provinces with Newfoundland. It is often said, particularly to our people of Nova Scotia: Had you not come into confederation, what would have become of you; what could you have done outside of confederation? Well, I desire to draw the attention of the house to the facts. In 1861, the year of the last census enumeration before confederation, Newfoundland had a population of 124,288; Prince Edward Island, 80,857; Nova Scotia, 330.857; New Brunswick, 252,047. The three maritime provinces combined at that time had an aggregate population of 663.751. In 1868, the year after confederation, it was estimated to be 771,799, and in 1921, 900,000. Now let me contrast with these figures the population of Newfoundland. In 1861, it was, as I have said, 124,288; in 1888, 131,000; and in 1921, 263 038. In other words, the percentage of increase over the same period in the case of Newfoundland was 112 per cent, while in the case of Nova Scotia it was under 60 per cent, and of New Brunswick under 54 per cent. Prince Edward Island actually lost population to the extent of 5 per cent as against Newfoundland more than doubling their population. The aggregate increase of the three maritime provinces was 36 per cent, contrasted with the 112 per cent increase of Newfoundland. Don't you think wTe could have got along had we of Nova Scotia remained without the Dominion of Canada? I make the assertion that the Dominion could not have been possible without the province of Nova Scotia; but Nova Scotia could have got along and done very well without confederation, measured by the experience of Newfoundland, where their resources are in no way comparable with those of my native province. Sir Andrew Rae Duncan refers to the fact that the people of Nova Scotia were able to take their place in regard to intelligence, energy and ability with the people of any of the other provinces. Reference has been made to the number of leading statesmen and professional men which Nova Scotia has supplied to the Dominion.
Now, a few weeks ago the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) made a considerable hullabaloo with reference to what one of his departments was doing in scientific research in the use of powdered fuels. I then

Steel Industry-Mr. Cantley
called his attention to the fact that that was an old story in Nova Scotia, where we had been using powdered fuel commercially and in an ordinary manufacturing way for at least fifteen years. Apparently in some directions about all that the minister's department does is to follow up, fifteen years later, work which has been successfully done by commercial companies and manufacturing institutions in other parts of the country. That is notably so with regard to the mining department of this government. A little later some reference was made in this house to a 6teamer which had made a round voyage from the United States to the old country under powdered fuel. That boat was the first boat in the world to be equipped with boilers fitted to burn powdered fuel. She is owned by the United States Shipping Board, but is operated by a private corporation. Now I hold in my hand a copy of the Morning Chronicle, of Halifax, the Nova Scotia organ of my good friends opposite, in which there appears a report of the trial trip of the steamer Lingan, owned in Nova Scotia by one of the coal companies, and recently equipped with a powdered fuel boiler installation. She is the first boat in the British Empire to have been so equipped, and the second in the world. The first boat so equipped, and to which I have already referred, was equipped by J. F. Page, the manager of the company operating the vessel. J. F. Page was the former superintendent of the Halifax shipyards, and is a son of Captain Page, a well known former shipmaster of River John, Pictou county and at one time in the employ of the Scotia Steel Company, New Glasgow. As I say, he is the man responsible for the first successful operation in the world of such an installation. The outcome of this venture, I have not the shadow of a doubt, will be that the cost of operating these coal boats will be considerably reduced, with this further advantage, that they will be operated entirely on slack coal which, as everyone knows, is today a more or less undesirable product. We use it of course in coking, but for powdered fuel it must be specially treated in exhaust-tube mills and reduced to a very fine powder about the consistency of talcum, with which some of my friends are perhaps familiar. I refer to this matter simply to show that we in Nova Scotia are not backward in any walk of life, and it is not to be suggested that for that cause the maritime provinces have occupied the position which they have unfortunately held for a considerable time.
The Duncan commission made a recommendation in regard to an additional payment, by way of subsidy, of the sum of $870,000.
This, they recommended, should be paid forthwith. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) last year told the house that he accepted that recommendation. The house rose in the latter days of April but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), with his Scotch caution, did not pay the amount forthwith; he paid one-half in July and the other half he paid only after some of those participating in the interprovincial conference, which met in the city of Ottawa, had protested against the non-payments of the money. And then, instead of paying the balance which was overdue, he wrongfully, in my judgment, withheld $130,000, being an amount in dispute in regard to a claim which then was and still is sub judiee. Are we not justified in Nova Scotia in feeling that we are not fairly treated? I put ft to the house, I put it to the minister himself: if he were in our place would he not complain? I take it he would.
My hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) has referred to the iron and steel industry; he has also made some reference to coal and coking plants. I told the house a year ago that the government's proposal in regard to a coking plant was of no use whatever to us. I repeat that statement, and I now wish to point out to hon. members what is taking place in Montreal. A large caking plant is being built there. Now, if the builders of that plant had had any intention of using domestic coal in connection with that installation they would have built the plant in or adjacent to the harbour of Montreal. But what have they done? They have built it on the canal bank where American coal can go directly to the plant, but where it is impossible to bring a ton of maritime coal except by transshipment by barges or railway cars. There is no possible doubt as to what their intention was; they located the plant in a place where it is practically impossible, due to transport charges, to use Nova Scotia coal. And that is all that this legislation will do in the way of assisting the coal industry of Nova Scotia. I pointed that out at the time, and my remarks in that regard have been amply justified by the evidence as stated.
So far as the iron and steel output of the country is concerned, it is unfortunately dwindling. Our March output was about 4 per cent below the output of the previous month. Our entire production of pig iron was only 74,000 tons, and of basic iron only 52,000 tons. In basic iron the amount was 22 per cent less than that of the previous month. The point to be noted is this: foundry iron is used simply for castings of various kinds-machinery castings,
Steel Industry-Mr. Cantley

stoves and goods of that sort. The progress of the steel industry is measured by the production of basic pig iron, which is used entirely for the production of steel; and the reduction in output of basic pig iron is, as I have stated, 22 per cent. It has been gradually falling off, while the importations of steel from the United States are increasing year by year and month by month.
I wish to make another appeal to the Minister of Finance to remedy the idiotic customs tariff schedule to which I called attention fifteen months ago. We have seventy items on the free list or with a 99 per cent rebate. Now what is the tariff board doing?-this precious tariff board appointed on the same day as the Duncan commission. What have they reported? If they have made a report the minister has not translated it into legislation. Let me point this out. The minister when appointing the Duncan commission told them that they might consider any extraneous related matter, that the door was wide open so fas as their investigation was concerned; they were not to regard it in any narrow or restricted way. They proceeded with the investigation and after it had been carried on for some time in Nova Scotia they came to Ottawa and were told by the then chairman of the tariff board that, so far as tariff matters were concerned, his board had charge of that feature and that the Duncan commission were not to be allowed to investigate anything touching the fiscal phase of the maritime question. I am disappointed that Sir Andrew Rae Duncan submitted to that attitude and to the curtailment of the scope of the inquiry; he should not have done so in view of the terms of his commission. However, he did, with the result that so far we have had no statement of any kind as to how tariff matters have affected the maritimes. We have no report, so far as we know, from the tariff commission to the minister. If they have reported, the minister has not so intimated to the house; and although the Duncan commission's report has been in the hands of the government since September, 1927, we still have no action as regards the iron and steel tariff or bounties as suggested by the Duncan commission. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) made reference to the question of the tariff and the bounty called for by the Duncan commission, which would be equivalent to the rebate of the duty on American fuel used in iron and steel making. Why has not that recommendation been implemented? A great deal has been said about the unrest in Nova Scotia.

The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) deals particularly with the implementing of the Duncan report and refers especially to the maritime provinces, but one part of that amendment deals with the iron and steel industry and has a much wider application than the remainder of the amendment. It is that particular section of the amendment to which I desire to refer. I do not intend to detain the house at any length, because I spoke on this question in the early part of the session and placed my views as fairly and as clearly as I could before the government. However, I feel that I would not be properly representing my constituency if I did not take advantage of this opportunity to express my regret that the government have not seen fit to bring in legislation at this session to improve the condition of the iron and steel industry in this country.
Some time ago I directed a question to the Minister of Finance in this connection, and his reply was that the matter was still under investigation by the tariff board. If that is the case it appears to me that it shows an amazing lack of interest on the part of someone . in not dealing with this matter more speedily, because it is more than two years since the question of iron and steel was submitted to the tariff board and surely in that period they have had ample time to conduct an investigation and make a report if they propose to do so.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there are aspects of this question with which the government should be able to deal without waiting for any report from the tariff board. I referred to some of these points when I spoke on the matter earlier in the session. For instance, the question of spring and axle steel is one which could be so considered; that steel is used in the manufacture of automobiles in this country and is being imported in very large quantities. We make spring and axle steel in Canada equal to that made in any

Steel Industry-Mr. Simpson
other country in the world, but the automobile manufacturers are allowed a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty paid on importations of that article, notwithstanding the fact that they enjoy a protection of from 20 per cent to 27-J per cent on their finished product. Surely it is not necessary to await the report of the tariff board to determine that that situation should 'be remedied. The minister has already admitted the principle, in speaking on the budget resolutions. The question of a certain grade of cotton yarn was under consideration; it had been free formerly but this year had a duty imposed upon it, and the minister was asked the reason for putting a duty on this article. His answer was that, this was the finished product of a certain factory and that finished product was the raw material of another factory in Canada which was enjoying protection, so his point was that this concern manufacturing the yarn should be entitled to a proportion of the protection. Why not apply the same principle to the spring and axle steel which is used in the manufacture of automobiles? That is all we are asking.
Another point which I brought to his attention at that time was the question of structural steel. At present structural steel weighing over 35 pounds to the yard is subject to a duty of 15 cents per hundred pounds, while structural steel weighing under 35 pounds to the yard is subject to a duty of 35 cents per hundred pounds. The steel weighing over 35 pounds is the larger shapes, and at the time that tariff item was framed none of those larger shapes were made in Canada, so we can readily understand the reason for the difference in the duty. To-day, however, several of these larger shapes are made in Canada, and some of our steel plants are prepared to manufacture practically all the larger shapes required in Canada if given reasonable protection. If the same degree of protection is afforded the larger structural shapes that now applies to those under 35 pounds to the yard I think we would speedily see activity in some of our steel manufacturing centres.

My hon. friend is referring now to the Algoma Steel Company, is
he not?

Would my hon. friend
permit a question just there? Some time ago another hon. member mentioned that commission, and I then asked if he could tell us how much had been paid by the Ontario government in bounties under the legislation or under whatever action was taken following that report. That hon. member could not tell me; does my hon. friend know?
The legislation was made subject to the Dominion government making provision for one-half the bounty.
Then no bounty has been paid by the Ontario government?

No. Until the Dominion government makes provision for one-half of the bounty I understand that the Ontario legislation does not become effective.
These are some of the conditions under which the steel industry is labouring to-day. One particular instance comes to my mind, that of Baldwin's Limited, one of the largest steel manufacturing concerns in the British Empire, who built a factory at Toronto for manufacturing certain classes of steel. Although they presented their case to the government at different times they received no assistance, and as a result closed their factory A little later on I will tell you where they are operating to-day.
Let us see what one of our sister dominions is doing in this regard. The Commercial Intelligence Journal of January 7, 1928, has the following article:
Australian Duties on Iron and Steel Products
In Commercial Intelligence Journal No. 1235 appeared a review of the principal Australian iron and steel industries down to a comparatively recent date. These companies have, for some time, contended that competition, particularly from the continent and to a lesser extent from the United Kingdom, was causing it to he unprofitable-under existing labour and wages conditions-to produce iron and steel products on the basis of a fair return for the capital invested.
The companies stressed that at least some of their processes of manufacture must perforce be discontinued, and many operatives thus thrown out of employment at a time when the country was experiencing the utmost difficulty in finding work for large numbers of men at
