speechtext:
Last evening at the adjournment of the house the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced that to-day we would go into supply and that among other departments we would take up the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals. I need not remind hon. gentlemen that the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals contain some items that are of great importance to the maritime provinces. My hon. friend (Mr. Cantley) who seconded the resolution this afternoon devoted considerable time to finding fault with us for what we had not done and he desired certain information from the Minister of Railways and Canals. In so doing he himself contributed for almost an hour to delaying the securing of the information, because the Minister of Railways and Canals when he comes down with his estimates will be prepared to give the house information that I am sure will not be opposed by the people of the maritime provinces. My hon. friends the mover and the seconder of the resolution laboured long and hard to convince themselves that they really have a grievance. They know better than that; they know that the people in the maritime provinces are not in sympathy with all these continual whinings for something more to be done in addition to what has already been done. I do not think they are helping their position very much with the electors of Canada, if we bear in mind all that we have already done in implementing the Duncan report, to delay continually the proceedings of parliament by harping upon this particular question.
The resolution presented to-day is in striking contrast-and I will come to that later- with the resolution on fiscal policy of the Tory party as presented at the Winnipeg convention. They are bolder to-day than they were when they were out on the prairies and I fancy they are bolder to-day even than they would be when they get down to the maritime provinces. The resolution centres about two particular items. One is an increased tariff, a higher duty on steel. I do
not think I am misrepresenling their position when I say that. The other is a bounty on steel and a bounty on coal. I am not very sure whether the hon. member for West Al-goma (Mr. Simpson), who presented, very fairly I am bound to say, the position of the great industry in his part of the country, is altogether in sympathy with the speeches delivered by my hon. friends from Nova Scotia. I am not sure that he is in favour of a bounty on coal going into the manufacture of steel. I should like the hon. gentleman, or someone else speaking for him to come out now and say whether he is in favour of a bounty on Canadian coal going into the manufacture of steel. I should like to have that point cleared up because it might help me later on to reach a conclusion when representatives of the different industries come before the Minister of Finance and the tariff board, as they came before. What did Sir Andrew Rae Duncan say in regard to the tariff on steel and the tariff on coal? Sir Andrew Rae Duncan knew his position; he knew that he was not the tariff commissioner for Canada, and he was very careful to state his position regarding the question of tariffs. I have under my hand the statement made by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan's board and in it I note the following:
Several features of the customs tariff in its relation to coal were brought to our attention, both by the government of Nova Scotia and by the operators of the coal mines.
Keep in mind that it was the government of Nova Scotia and the operators of the coal mines who brought this to their attention.
These we feel ourselves precluded from dealing with, since they are a matter properly to be considered by the tariff advisory board; but we may be permitted to say that we are' impressed with the need for reconsideration of the customs tariff in its relation to coal, anthracite and coke, and we recommend that the tariff advisory board should be asked to give immediate consideration to the subject.
That is as far as Sir Andrew Rae Duncan went in his report. He recommended that the tariff advisory board should give immediate attention to the question.
Have they done so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to that in a
moment. Sir Andrew Duncan stated further:
It was submitted that the tendency of the tariff, as affected by successive alterations, has been to lessen the protection upon the primary products of iron and steel and to encourage their importation from other countries as being the raw materials of iron and steel-fabricating and finishing industries in Canada.
Steel Industry-Mr. Robb

What did Sir Andrew Duncan say about
that? He said:
In respect of this matter, we da not conceive it to be onr duty to express any opinion, since the question is, as we were informed by the chairman of the tariff advisory board, who met us at our request, at the present moment under the consideration of that board.
How long ago was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is from the Duncan
report.
That is two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Two applications were made
to the Minister of Finance to consider the iron and steel duties and the coal duties. One was made by that great corporation of the maritime provinces known as Besco, the British Empire Steel Corporation. The other was made by that company in the riding of the hon. member for West Algoma, the Algoma Steel Corporation. Those applications were made to the Minister of Finance in May, 1926, and at that time the first hearing was had on the applications. At the first public hearing the applicants appeared before the tariff board and they represented that they were under severe competition, particularly from overseas countries. Representatives of the tariff board were sent out to inquire into the allegations made before the board by these two great steel companies, the British Empire Steel Corporation and the Algoma Steel Corporation; but what happened? It was not very long after that until the British Empire Steel Corporation got into litigation; they became involved in a lawsuit, and the tariff board realized, from the attitude of the companies, the division of opinion that existed between the different parts of the companies, that they could not get very far and that no good purpose could be served by continuing the inquiry until after the question was settled. The question was prolonged for some time in the courts and eventually it was settled. The British Empire Steel Corporation was put into the hands of a receiver and under the receiver the management of the company has been so much better that the company is making greater progress than it did under the old management. I am not prepared to say that this is all due to the more efficient management because, as operators of the plant in Nova Scotia, they had pretty efficient management; but the receiver employed good salesmen who went out after business, and I am going to be able to show in a few moments that they secured more business. The tariff board has been waiting until this question was settled

to have a further inquiry before it on the applications of the two great companies, the British Empire Steel Corporation and the Algoma Steel Corporation.
But they started something larger than they had imagined. When their application for a higher tariff on iron and steel and coal came before the tariff advisory board for a first hearing, then all the other industries throughout Canada that were interested in that question began to send in requests to the Minister of Finance for a hearing before the board, and the result is that there are now throughout Canada 350 firms interested in this application which originated in May, 1926, and they all want to get a hearing before the tariff board. I can quite understand how my hon. friends argue this afternoon that they would like to have this question settled here in parliament, rather than have to go before the tariff advisory board. I think they ars speaking by the book. I think they are speaking perhaps for some of these big corporations, because no later than April 19 of this year the chairman of the tariff advisory board was advised by the receiver for Besco that they were not interested very much in pushing this tariff application at the present moment. That is why the delay is taking place. The tariff advisory board is anxious to go on with the inquiry, and the government are anxious for the inquiry to go on because we want to get this question cleaned up, but the original applicant, the Besco, I say to my hon. friends who come from that part of the country, have declared that they are not just ready to go on with the inquiry, and they are not pressing the application before the board at this moment. That is why the board has not yet reported.
My hon. friend from West Algoma this afternoon presented the situation as it exists in Australia, with regard to the tariffs which they have recently introduced on iron and steel. But Australia has had a high tariff on iron and steel for some years, and the industry of Australia to-day is suffocated because of the high tariff they have on iron and steel and on other products, and the great mining industry of Australia has been practically standing idle for some time. I observe that my hon. friends hope that by higher and higher tariffs they are going to resuscitate this great industry in Australia, but if I read the press of Australia correctly, the Australians are beginning to think that they are top-heavy with tariff, and that their industries are suffering more from high tariff than from anything else.

Steel Industry-Mr. Robb
Then can the minister explain why Baldwin's, Limited, have closed their factory in Canada and gone to Australia, if high tariff is a deterring factor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Baldwin's got hold of a plant in Canada that was used for making munitions; they got it at a bargain. They had made a lot of money out of it during the war, but I do not think they ever opened that plant since. They had bought it for a song, thinking that they might operate it, but after looking into the matter, they decided not.
They operated for a year on sheets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows, and I will accept his statement.
The Duncan commission in its survey of the iron and steel industry of the maritime provinces had before them the statistics of that industry for the year 1925, because the commission was sitting during the summer of 1926, and it was only reasonable to suppose that when they were inquiring into that industry they would look up the general statistics of the iron and steel industry of Canada, because my hon. friends must remember that there are other provinces in Canada that are interested in the iron and steel industry besides the province of Nova Scotia. Now, what were the conditions in 1925? I find from the reports of the Bureau of Statistics for the year 1927 that the number of employees in the iron and steel industry increased from 1925 by 15 600; in other words, there are 15.000 more employees in the iron and steel industry throughout all Canada than there were in 1925.

Will the minister allow me to correct him? I am quite sure he does not intend to mislead the house, but the figures that he is giving take in all the subsidiary industries that use iron and steel. They do not deal simply with the primary products.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly, and the government has to do with all the iron and steel industries throughout this great Dominion. We cannot legislate for one industry alone.

You
have done it in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, we are not doing it now In 1925 the total number of employees in the iron and steel industry, as given by the Bureau of Statistics, was 90,125.
That includes all subsidiary iron and steel working and fabricating shops small and large through Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Taking in all the industries, and in 1927 the number was 105,782. The selling value of the products of the iron and steel industry in 1925 was $411,378,640, and in 1927, $515,971,445.
My hon. friend a few moments ago complained of conditions in the coal industry in Nova Scotia. Well, in 1928, when the Duncan commission were considering the coal industry, they had before them the statistics for 1925, and I find that there were engaged in the coal industry of Nova Scotia-I am quoting now the sort of figures that will please my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley)-8,333 employees and in 1927, there were 13,975 employees in that great industry.

There
was a strike in 1925.
Quote a normal year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am quoting the year which the Duncan commission had before them But I will take another year. The number of employees in that great industry in 1926 was 12,100, and in 1927, 13,975.
While my hon. friend is quoting statistics, will he give the importations of iron and steel into this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not that before me. but my hon. friend will find it on the record; it was quoted a moment ago.
I know it quite well. It was $250,000,000 in one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then why ask the question?
The minister is putting on the record figures that suit him, and I would like the other side put on the record at the same time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are more people engaged in the iron and steel industry throughout Canada to-day than there were in 1925.
And more people engaged in foreign countries producing the same kind of products.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, you are getting pretty far away from the Winnipeg convention. You had at the Winnipeg convention a few sane men who were determined not to get the great Conservative party into a position where they would be strangling the industries of this country, and they framed a resolution. I think I know who framed this particular resolution. I did not sit oprevised EDITION
Steeh Industry-Mr. Robb

posite that gentleman for a few years without being able to recognize his style. Here is the resolution:
This convention desires to record its feeling of pride in the growth and progress and prosperity of Canada, under the historic fiscal policy of the Liberal-Conservative party.
It affirms its adherence to the principles of that policy in its declared objects of stimulating the development of the natural resources of the Dominion: preserving and enlarging the market for Canadian farm products; building up the industries of Canada, and thus creating employment for our workmen, promoting interprovincial trade, and generally providing a diversified economic life -which will be effectual in retaining Canada's sons and daughters within our own boundaries.
As to tariff revisions the convention declared :
In such revisions regard should be had not only to the objects of fiscal policy herein enumerated, but to the welfare of the consumer, and it is desirable in the national interest that in such revisions the cost of living and the cost of the implements used in production, of whatever nature, should be given special and attentive study with a view to the reduction of such costs to the extent practicable.
That is a pretty sound position. Now my hon. friend a moment ago advocated bounties. He said: We want higher duty and bounties, but if we cannot get both we want bounties. I recall the attitude of the Conservative party on bounties. I have before me a speech made by a pretty good minister of finance, Sir Thomas White. In his budget speech of 1914 he said:
My own view is that bounties are justifiable to call into being new industries where capital, which is always timid as to experimental ventures, requires special inducement to enter upon their development, but after such enterprises have been called into being and firmly established, it is difficult to justify further aid of a direct character.
That was the view of Sir Thomas White when he was Minister of Finance.

What was Mr. Fielding's
view?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Fielding introduced
bounties for this parent industry to get it started, but as the years progressed he allowed them to lapse, and he had exactly the same view as Sir Thomas White, that when an industry got going it should be able to stand on its own feet.
My hon. friends have referred to the question of reciprocal trade, and although they have not emphasized it very much to-day, I observed from some of the preceding speeches that they were very strong on doing something for the maritime provinces by way of getting larger and better markets for their

natural products. I wonder what their policy is to-day. I know the voters in the maritimes are sound on this; they have learned a lesson. But what is the attitude of the Tory party? Is it the same attitude as the party had in 1911? I think it is important that before this debate closes we should know just exactly where the Tory party stand on this question.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to
a question of privilege. I belong to the Liberal-Conservative party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were a good many
people in the constituency of my hon. friend who were not just sure where he belonged during the election.
They know now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not going over the
various votes that have been put through to implement the recommendations of the Duncan report, but I observe that the supply bill is practically padded with votes for the maritime provinces.
Not in my county.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know what county
my hon. friend comes from; but notwithstanding the complaints made this afternoon regarding certain warehouses down in Prince Edward Island, I observe that for Georgetown we voted $54,000 odd for the reconstruction of a wharf and frostproof warehouse; for dredging $16,448, and for additional dredging $7,650. With respect to Summerside there has been voted for reconstruction of wharf, $58,497, for dredging $4,972, and for additional dredging $5,400. For Charlottetown there has been voted for the reconstruction of wharf, contract now awarded, $136,000 and for dredging $63,000 odd. So I submit to my hon. friends that the little province of Prince Edward Island has not been badly treated by this government. We have gone a long way, as my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) will prove in a few moments, to implement the recommendations of the Duncan report.
What about the recommendations in that report with regard to the ports in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick? Surely hon. gentlemen opposite have not forgotten their own obstruction when my colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) was trying to put through the different bills for harbours.

There was no obstruction.

Steel Industry-Mr. Robb
Mr. ROBB. There was obstruction in dealing with the Quebec harbour bill which delayed us getting down to the bills relating to St. John and Halifax harbours.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Eventually we got down to
the ports of the maritime provinces, and there we advanced $500,000 to one and $5,000,000 to the other.

May I remind the hon.
minister that I have upheld the ruling made by those who have preceded me in the chair, that an hon. member cannot accuse another hon. member of obstructing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I shall have to use the word "delay". Now, a moment ago my hon. friend complained regarding the additional vote for subsidies to the maritime provinces. As hon. gentlemen will recall, in the estimates last session there were provided additional votes of $875,000 to Nova Scotia, $600,000 to New Brunswick and $125,000 to Prince Edward Island. Similar amounts are in the estimates this year to be again voted. My hon. friend complains because the Department of Finance did not go directly contrary to the statute and pay out these votes in a lump sum. We paid out these subsidies as we always do, semi-annually. We made the first payment regularly, and when the representatives of the interprovincial conference met here in Ottawa I think two of them made this representation to us:	Our annual year
ends the last of November:	We wonder if
you could let us have that money before the first of January. They recognized that it was not due until that date. They were reasonable men. We said:	Yes, we have the
money and we will make the payments a few days in advance to help you out. But those gentlemen recognized that the Dominion treasury was under no obligation to make the payments earlier than we had made the preceding payments.
What was the wording of the Duncan report in that regard; was it not that an immediate iilterim lump sum should be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, the word "immediate"
was not there. Another point hon. members from the maritimes might very well keep in mind. At the interprovincial conference to which I have referred not one of the representatives of the larger provinces made any objection to giving this additional grant to the maritime provinces.

Because they had no right
to.
Why should they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not one had any objection.
An hon. MEMBER. Why should they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The government intend to
reconsider these subsidies and place them on a proper basis. What more need I say? My hon. friend finds fault because the tariff advisory board have not yet reported. The fact of the matter is that the main industry in his own province is delaying the inquiry by the board. No one could be more anxious to go on with the inquiry and clean up the matter before next session than the members of the government and of the tariff advisory board.

May I ask the minister a
question on the steel industry? The Financial Post of April 20 contains a news item that the government had given a promise to the steel industry that if they could get past the gauntlet of western criticism the government would give them something next year on which the industry could be built up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I read that article, and if my recollection is correct the article did not state it in the words my hon. friend has indicated. It was a feeler", put out as an ordinary news item; it was a feeler, I admit. But they did not say specifically that the government had made any promise to them, and if they made that statement they are wrong; the government has made no promise to them. The government has referred this steel inquiry to the tariff advisory board. Some 350 other firms throughout Canada have said, "We want to be heard on this; we are interested. We employ more labour in the steel and iron industry than do the two large steel industries, and we want to be heard". As a matter of fact, in the steel and iron industry of Canada, but 4 per cent are employed in the province of A ova Scotia. I ask, has the government to give no consideration to the other 96 per cent? Have we not some interest in doing what we can, what is reasonable, what the country will support, to keep these other industries throughout Canada employing labour, paying good wages, and thus keeping them as prosperous as they are now?
In conclusion, all I have to say is this. The government are sympathetic to the great iron and steel industry of Canada. We have shown that sympathy, having due regard to all other industries in Canada. And the steel
3268	COMMONS
Steel Industry-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
industry themselves having elected to go before the tariff board, we say to them, "Gentlemen, you must appear before that board and have this inquiry made before next session".
Is my hon, friend aware that the Halifax Herald advertised and asked us to visit the prosperous province of Nova Scotia?

It is not my purpose to detain the house very long in the few remarks I wish to make. Miay I say, first, that I associate myseilf with the mover and seconder of this amendment.
Before taking up what I had in mind discussing in this connection, may I refer for a minute or two to some observations made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), who has just taken his seat. Towards the end of his address he was asked by the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) whether the word "immediate" was not in the Duncan report in reference to the lump sum payments recommended to be paid the maritime provinces; and the Minister of Finance said that the word "immediate" was not in the report. I have in my hand a copy of the report and at page 19 I find this:
And accordingly we recommend that immediate interim lump-sum increases-
The Minister of Finance said the word "immediate" was not there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Read the whole thing.
Immediate increases.
Exactly; but the Minister of Finance said that the word "immediate" was not there.
He said "immediate payment" was not there.

That is a rare variety of quibbling with which I am not acquainted. The report states:
We recommend that immediate interim lumpsum increases should be made in the payments to the three maritime provinces as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was done.

Not only that, but the Minister of Finance misled the house with reference to what the Interprovincial conference did with regard to the non-payment of these subsidies. My information is that the Minister of Finance was called before the conference, because those who were there, from all over the Dominion, resented the fact that these subsidies had not been paid in full.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend let me nail that right now. It is but fair to the ministers from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to say that there was nothing of the kind. They came to me quietly and wanted to know whether we were in funds and could let them have the money, so that their books would make a beter showing at the end of the year.
I accept the minister's word immediately. My information was to the contrary.
Where from?

From those
who came representing the province of Nova Scotia.
From the ministers concerned?
You look at the records, as you said to someone else this afternoon, and you will find the names of those representing Nova Scotia at the Interprovincial conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that either Premier Rhodes or Mr. Harrington made that statement?

I have made the statement and I leave it to the Minister of Finance to put whatever interpretation he likes on it. The statement stands.
Now, the Minister of Finance seemed to be annoyed and agitated at the fact that we were holding up the house for a few hours to discuss the question of steel and coal in the province of Nova Scotia. We have been waiting since confederation for fair play in Nova Scotia, and neither the Minister of Finance nor any other member on the other side of the house has any right to get up and complain because we occupy a few hours in order to put our claims before this honourable body. Another point the Minister of Finance made was that we were whining with regard to what had not been done. If we are whining-
Hear, hear.

Someone on the other side say "hear, hear". If we are whining, the boards of trade all over Nova Scotia are whining. They have sent resolutions to every member from Nova Scotia complaining that the Duncan report had not been implemented in full; and I am sure the bouse will be surprised to know that one of these resolutions was signed by the president of the Liberal association of Nova Scotia.

Steel Industry-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
If we are doing a little whining in connection with the matter, whining has been done by others in Nova Scotia as well.
The Minister of Finance also went into the question of the high tariff wall on iron and steed in the commonwealth of Australia and stated that they were ready to abandon that high tariff because they thought it was interfering with their business in that country; and he made some odious comparisons between Australia and Canada. If you want to get at the basis of the development of the steel industry in any country, the most glowing example is the United States. When they established their steel industry they put their tariff high enough to shut out all competition. And what are we up against in Canada? A few days ago I saw in the newspaper that we imported $300,000,000 of iron and steel products in the last year, while our own steel industry, one of the primary industries in this country, is idle-t'he foundries in Sydney and other places in Nova Scotia, for instance. It does not seem to me that the policy of this government is one that is of much benefit to the steel and iron industry or to the Dominion of Canada, when we have to send three hundred millions of our good dollars annually over to the United States, importing steel and iron products into this country.
There is another point in connection with this steel industry. The primary steel industry of Canada enjoys a protection of less than 10 per cent, while the other steel industries-the finished product-enjoy a protection of around 30 per cent. We are trying to struggle along with a protection of under 10 per cent; and the way we are struggling is tragic, sending $300,000,000 a year to other countries for iron and steel products.
Are the dollars there?
I suppose they are there; they were sent there. I think they usually keep what they get.

That is more than all
Canadian currency.

You can suit yourself if you can get comfort out of that. Now, we in supporting this amendment are not merely speaking our own minds when we advocate the implementing of the Duncan report in toto; we are voicing the sentiments of the people of the maritime provinces. We are not at all ashamed to come forward and say that we were promised that this report would be implemented in full, and we certainly know in the maritimes that it has not been implemented in full. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), making a statement in
the house last year, implied that the report, with regard to steel and coal, would be implemented in full as soon as the big steel and coal company question was decided and the lita-gation settled. These things have all taken place, yet we are nearing the end of another session of parliament with no legislation brought down and nothing done to implement the Duncan report in that particular. The Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), speaking in the city of St. John last fall, said that what the government was going to do for the steel industry in the province of Nova Scotia during the coming sesssion would make every citizen of the maritime provinces proud. Well, we have waited to see what was to be done, but up to the present nothing has been done and from the remarks of the Minister of Finance I judge that nothing will be done, because I rather took it from his remarks that he considered we were getting more than we were entitled to at present.

They will recommend it to
the Civil Service Commission.

Yes, or perhaps to the tariff board. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have to refer to only one other matter, and that is the question of coal. During the present session I placed a question on the order paper asking if the Canadian National Railways owned a coal company in the United States. The answer was that they did, that it was taken over when the assets of the Grand Trunk Railway were taken over by the Canadian National Railway. In that same answer I found that this company supply coal to Canada to the extent of about 300,000 tons annually. It seems to me that this government has not grasped the true national spirit with respect to coal and steel in Canada. I have given the figures with respect to the money sent to the United States to bring steel to this country, and it is well known that a tremendous sum of money, over $100,000,000 yearly, is sent to that country to bring coal to Canada. It is also a well known fact that many of our coal miners and steel workers are out of employment but still the Canadian National Railways, which is a branch of this government, owned by the Dominion of Canada, operates a coal mine in the United States and sells coal back to our Canadian people; probably it is used on the Canadian National railway. I believe that in justice to the people of this country the Canadian National Railways should be instructed by this government to dispose of property of that kind in the United States, which is being operated in direct competition with our own coal mines and to the detriment of our coal miners in Canada.
$270	COMMONS
(Steel Industry-Mr, Macdonald (Kings)
And they handled more business than ever.

Yes, I would like to quote from a report given out on April 3 by W. U. Appleton, general manager of the Atlantic region:
From the date of the opening of the shipping season in October last to the 31st of March, this year, the Canadian National Railways car ferry has moved from Prince Edward Island to the mainland over 1,000 more carloads of potatoes than were carried across in the season of 1926-27. Up to March 31st, inclusive, there were 3,832 carloads of potatoes ferried from the island province; for the same period last season there were 2,781, thus an increase of 1,051 carloads. Before the shipments of this season are completed the total will have reached 4,000, if not exceeding that number.

speechtext:
When the house was in committee the other night I spoke for about five minutes in opposition to the bill. This bill has been a football in parliament for some years. When the bill was reported back to the house, we had quite a debate on it. This particular company has been coming to parliament for many years seeking favours. In my opinion this bill is a sample of the way in which insurance companies have been playing fast and loose with the legislation of the country and the sooner we have a new insurance act making it compulsory for all these companies to be under sound public control, the better. This particular company came to parliament first away back in 1865 and got a charter under chapter 43 of the statutes of that year. It came back in 1870 and got another act passed, chapter 58, along the same lines. Not satisfied with that it came back again in 1871 and got another act passed, chapter 53. It came back again in 1882, when chapter 100 of the statutes was passed and again in 1897 when chapter 82 of the statutes was passed. Now it comes along with this bill No. 56, section 1 of which reads:
The capital of the company shall be five million dollars, and the unissued portion thereof may be issued from time to time by the directors in such amounts as they may deem in the interests of the company.
Clause 2 of the bill provides:
Except as hereinafter provided no sums in excess of twenty-five per cent of the amount subscribed thereon shall be called by the directors or received by the company as payment on account of any shares of the capital stock which may be hereafter issued, except under the authority of and in accordance with the terms of such general enactment, if any, as may be passed by the parliament of Canada dealing with all life insurance companies which have
TMr. Church.]
a capital stock and derive their powers from the said parliament of Canada, unless the capital of the said company should at any time become impaired, as defined in subsection two of section seventy of the Insurance Act, or the company should in any year fail to declare dividends to the holders of its participating policies.
In the explanatory note on the opposite page of the bill it is pointed out that subsection 2 of section 70 of the Insurance Act reads as follows:
The capital of a company shall be deemed to be impaired when its assets, exclusive of its paid-up capital', are less than its liabilities calculated according to the requirements of this act.
I would point out, Mr, Speaker, that the Superintendent of Insurance was opposed to this bill. Then by clause 3 it is provided that the par value of the shares shall be $10. We all know what an increase that will mean.
Then clause 4 distinguishes between different classes of shares, and provides for the approval of the transfer of the shares.
Clause 5 deals with the surrender or exchange of the shares, and the underlined portion of clause 5 reads:
as many fully paid shares of "Class B" stock as may be by said by-law provided, but the paid-up value of the shares of "Class B" stock which may be so given as payment or in exchange shall not exceed by more than twenty-five per cent the paid up value of the shares surrendered. The shares thus surrendered shall ipso facto become "Class B" stock and may be reissued as such by the company.
So by legislation they are going to change one class of security for another, and we are being asked to interfere with the ordinary commercial transactions of the sales of the shares of this company.
Clause 6 deals with the sale of shares to employees and policyholders, and according to an explanatory note in the bill as reprinted the words " but not more than one hundred of such shares may be so sold to any. one person," at the end of section 6 are omitted, at the expense, no doubt, of the policyholders, as has been done before, and for the benefit of the shareholders.
Clause 7 provides that the stock qualification of a director shall be twenty-five shares of the capital stock.
I wish to protest, Mr. Speaker, against the passing of this bill. I do not think it is in the public interest that this house should lend itself to passing this class of legislation. I have a motion of which I have given notice already for the six months' hoist. Canada has been a very happy hunting ground for the Sun Life Company. Talk about what the Sun Life has done for Canada; what has Canada done for the Sun Life? The com-

Hun Life Company
pany has taken away the premiums paid in by those policyholders who have allowed their policies to lapse. If a soldier who has come back from the war finds himself out of work and unable to pay his premiums, then the company, if his policy has not run for three years, keep all the money he has paid in, and what this and other life companies receive in this way runs into hundreds of thousands of dollars. The Sun Life is not investing its money to develop Canada alone, but it has investments all over the civilized world. The, company is a law unto itself. It comes to parliament and gets amendments to its charter which are not within the four corners of the general Insurance Act or sound insurance. There should be a national policy evolved with respect to insurance and for the regulation of insurance companies. A resolution was introduced into this house two years ago with regard to the way in which not only this company but many other insurance companies are able to evade the law not only with regard to lapsed policies, but in regard to their general business policy all along the line we need a national insurance policy. More restrictions should be placed in the Insurance Act, or the act will be more effective than the Bank Act was some years ago. I do not suggest that this particular company is to blame, because it is in a good financial position and I believe it is well managed, but I do object to this parliament passing legislation of this kind for the benefit of a company which utilizes its money, not for the development of Canada alone particularly, but for investment purposes all over the world to suit its own purposes.

The hon. member who moved that the bill be reported knew perfectly well not only that the bill was a contentious one, but that amendments have been proposed against it, and therefore I wish to protest vigorously against this sort of procedure.
Vn e all admit that the Sun Life is a very large company, and that it has done well for its policyholders, but I do not know that it has done more for its policyholders than many other companies; in fact, I do not think it has done quite so much.
We are also told that this company is a great asset to this country. I would like to ask, what makes a company of any description a great asset to any country? I would think that it was because of one of three things. I would say that this company was a great asset to this country if it insured a large number of our citizens at a reasonable rate. Or it might be a great asset if it distributed profits to a large number of shareholders. Or it might be a great asset to this country if it invested a large amount of its money in Canadian industry. If any of these three things were true with regard to the Sun Life, I would say that it was a great asset to this country, but what do we find? With regard to issuing insurance at reasonable rates, I am informed on the best of authority that its terms are no better than those of the average life insurance company, and not as good as some. Furthermore, instead of insuring the Canadian public in large numbers, I find that only a very small percentage of this company's business is done in Canada. According to a statement of my hon. friend who sits near me, the hon. member for 'St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), which will be found at page 2412 of Hansard of 1927, sixty-three per cent of the business of this company was at that time done outside of Canada, and possibly seventy-five per cent of its business will be done outside this country within a year's time. According to correspondence now made public between the president of this company and the Insurance department, an even greater percentage of the business of this company is done outside Canada.
With regard to distributing its profits to its shareholders, here again we find a weakness, because the shareholders are not so very many after all. Out of 20,000 shareholders, we find that 51 shareholders control no less than 13,928 shares, while 524 shareholders control only 6,074 shares. So on that ground the company falls down in being a great asset to this country. In the third place, how much of this company's money is invested in Canada? This is a very important point, because we are everlastingly hearing of the need of bringing capital into this country. With regard to the capital of this company and its investments, I was surprised to find that although it claims to be such an asset to Canada-it has invested its funds very largely in other countries. Now, if the company has so much at heart the interests of Canada, why does it not invest its capital in Canadian industries? Instead of doing this, we find that in the United States alone the company is interested in no less than 233 American concerns, and its foreign investments total over two hundred million dollars.

When the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the royal commission's report. I was showing how the transportation recommendations in connection with Prince Edward Island had not been carried out, particularly in regard to the standardization of the roadbed, and the ferry steamer. I was arriving at the point where I was endeavouring to show the increased traffic which had taken place during the past few years, and emphasizing the fact that the need for a second car ferry had arisen on account of the increase in traffic itself, regardless of any other condition.
Prince Edward Island was induced to go into confederation by the promise of a continuous and efficient steam service-mark the word "efficient"-being established and maintained between the island and the mainland winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the railway systems of the Dominion. Until this car ferry went into service about the year 1915 no reasonable attempts had been made by the various governments to implement this promise. For five, six, seven and eight weeks we had been isolated from the mainland, without any connection whatever by steam, as promised under the terms of confederation. The car ferry did very well for a time, and gave what might fairly be regarded as efficient service. After all, "efficient" is a comparative term, and what might be efficient to-day might not be efficient to-morrow. That is what has happened to the car ferry; she was efficient when she undertook this service, but the traffic has increased to such an extent that it is physically impossible for one boat to handle it. Consequently the need for a second car ferry, as recommended by the Duncan commission, has become acute.
3278	COMMONS
Steel Industry-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
In addition to the fact that the need is quite apparent from the standpoint of increased traffic, there is another aspect of it which is perhaps even more important. This matter was referred to by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) this afternoon, and I will not attempt to cover the ground he did in connection with the danger to a single boat. This boat has to fight heavy ice day and night for months at a time, and every person will realize the great strain which that causes. The boat is now thirteen years old, and is liable to accident at any time.
This is the only channel of communication with the island, and the matter, therefore, is vital. Should anything happen in the-winter time which would result in the interruption of communication we might reach the point where we would have to face cold and hunger on Prince Edward Island. Before this car ferry was put into operation the merchants all over the province stocked up big sheds full of coal and warehouses full of foodstuffs of all kinds to carry through the winter, in anticipation of being tied up from six to eight weeks. That system is now a thing of the past. We no longer stock up for winter needs; we depend on having a steady stream of coal cars, flour cars, feed cars for our stock, and all other necessities coming through day by day on this car ferry. It an accident happened to that boat we would be faced with cold and hunger. I do not think I need go any further along this line; but in view of the large expenditures which are being made by the government in various directions, some of which are not at all necessary or at all events not nearly so necessary as this, the government should at this session of parliament have inserted in the supplementary estimates an item which will take care of the needs of Prince Edward Island in this regard.
The car ferry steamer cannot be built in a month or a year. Supposing an item is inserted in the estimates this session, the earliest date at which we could expect to have a second boat would be probably the fall of 1929. I am not speaking in any critical or political sense; I have already expressed my appreciation of the work that the railway management has done, and before closing I wish to finish a quotation, which I had started to read before six o'clock, from a statement made by Mr. Appleton, general manager of the Atlantic region, in connection with the difficulty of serving the province under present conditions. Mr. Appleton said:
Everything that is at all possible is being done to facilitate the movements of potatoes

from Prince Edward Island and the shipments by the car ferry of the Canadian National this year are greater than at any time in the history of the road.
He went on to say:
Whatever shortage of cars there may have been at times they W'ere caused by such circumstances that were quite beyond our control.
He said further that during the present season more than 4,000 empty refrigerator cars had to be ferried across in order to carry away potatoes from Prince Edward Island. He said further:
While providing this service for Prince Edward Island we were also endeavouring to meet demands for refrigerator cars from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec which demands in the aggregate are equal to the requirements of Prince Edward Island.
That will give hon. members some idea of the situation with which a single car ferry has to cope. According to Mr. Appleton, as many refrigerator cars are required in Prince Edward Island as in the three large provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec combined.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman will explain what relevancy his remarks have to the amendment before the chair. I should think they would be more relevant in a debate that might take place on the items in the estimates when considered by the committee of the whole house. I do not just at present see the relevancy of his remarks.

The Duncan
'Commission which was under discussion this afternoon gives as one of its recommendations:
Prince Edward Island car ferry.-The terms and conditions upon which Prince Edward Island was admitted into confederation in 1873 contained the following provisions: -
"Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of tile Dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the Dominion".
It goes on to say:
The present car ferry affords a much improved service as compared with that which the island formerly enjoyed, but in recent years traffic and freight have considerably increased, and will continue to increase, particularly at certain seasons of the year.
An so on. I was discussing the car ferry service.
Of course the main argument was about the steel industry. The hon. gentleman was discussing the Duncan report generally. That explains the relevancy of his remarks.

I understood that the amendment referred to the report

Steel Industry-Mr. Church
of the Duncan commission. I was discussing the demands on the car ferry. Mr. Appleton further stated that at one time there were 400 unfilled requisitions for refrigerator cars for potatoes. Hon. members will realize that when there is a ready and good market for perishable products, if you cannot get them moved the chances are that you will lose heavily, and that is what has happened.
As I said a moment ago, I am not speaking in a critical or political sense; I am speaking for the purpose of making as sincere, honest and earnest a request as I can to the Minister of Railways and to the government to provide those much needed facilities and, as regards the car ferry, a vital need for the people of Prince Edward Island, not only because of the recommendations of the Duncan commission but because the honour of the parliament of Canada in regard to the terms of confederation is at a stake. If there had neveT been a Duncan commission, we would have had a right to insist on account of the terms of confederation itself.

The resolution of the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) calls upon the government to implement in full the recommendations contained in the Duncan report, particularly the recommendation relating to the steel industry. That hon. gentleman in my opinion is correct in the statements that he has made. This is not the first time that we have had a recommendation from a commission or a committee of this house; we had commissions or coal committees appointed in 1923, 1924, 1925 and 1926 to consider the industries of steel and coal in the maritime provinces. Those industries in the maritime provinces are in a precarious and withering state. The coal and steel industries all over the whole world are in a precarious state to-day owing to the disturbance of the industrial equilibrium after the war and owing to economic conditions. The maritime provinces have been suffering for many years on this account and hon. members on this side have been for five or six years bringing this coal and steel matter to the attention of parliament. Recommendations have been made but not one of them has been implemented.
You cannot deal with the steel industry in the maritimes without considering the allied coal industry; they are one. The amendment calls for implementing in full the recommendations of the Duncan report, particularly in regard to the steel industry. There is only one way in which to solve the ills of those two basic industries in this country and that
is the way in which they solved them in England after the war. When England found that she was losing to the Hamburg yards the steel, coal and ship building orders, what did the Baldwin government do? They adopted exactly what those on this side of the house have been arguing for in season and out of season, namely, a safeguarding of industries act in the way of subsidies, bonuses and subventions, so as to give proper protection for those two industries. That is a system of subventions, subsidies and bonuses, which is the backbone of the Duncan report for the relief of the maritime provinces. Coming from Ontario I may say that central Ontario is clamouring for steel and coal from the maritime provinces, but owing to the difficulty of transportation and the high freight rates on the water and rail or all-rail routes for the cartage of coal and steel to central Canada, the maritime provinces are losing hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of tenders. In the city from which I come they found in some cases that these commodities in parts could be brought in duty paid cheaper than they could be brought from the maritime provinces owing to the heavy freight rate, both by all-rail or water and rail routes.
When this report was before the house last year I understood that the house was unanimous in regard to it. It deals specifically with the question of the Nova Scotia iron and steel industry. That question is one of vital importance, and one which must be considered not only on provincial grounds but also on national grounds, and on the ground of empire considerations as well. On provincial grounds it is of very great importance to Nova Scotia, because around and about that industry there have grown up many of the most populous centres in that province. The city of Sydney, and the towns of North Sydney, Sydney Mines, New Glasgow, Trenton and Stellarton, with very substantial populations, are all entirely dependent for their very existence on the success or failure of the Nova Scotia steel industry. They furnish the principal home market for the agricultural products of the farmers for many miles surrounding these towns.
May I point out also that there is an interdependence between the Nova Scotia steel industry and the Nova Scotia coal industry. When working at full capacity the Nova Scotia steel industry is capable of consuming, and does consume, over a million tons of Nova Scotia coal per year. You can see, Mr. Speaker, how very important to the province of Nova Scotia is the welfare of this industry in respect of which we are asking the government for assistance. We are asking not for any special assistance but for that assistance which was recommended by a tribunal of their own creation.
This is a question which should appeal to every hon. member of this house on national grounds. If you will look into the industrial history of those nations which are to-day pre-eminent in wealth, in power and in population, you will find that every one of them owes that pre-eminent position to a careful fostering of its coal and steel industries. We in this country in the years that are to come, no matter what government may be in power -although the continuation in power of my hon. friends opposite may somewhat retard industrial progress-are bound to achieve a great industrial expansion. In not so many years we will have a highly industrialized country. Wei will have opportunities for employment, not for ten million but probably for one hundred million people. We will have myriads of opportunities for employment for our own sons and daughters, and for many others who come from foreign lands. We must be careful, therefore, to foster and protect those industries which are of national and basic importance, which are wrapped up with the industrial future of this country.
We who sit in these seats to-night are not legislating merely for our own generation, nor for this year; we must not look through the eyes of years or of decades. In dealing with national problems we must look through the eyes of centuries; we must follow those policies which, while at present involving perhaps some sacrifice, in the course of years will redound to the industrial and political advantage of our country. No nation which has attained a pre-eminent position in respect of population or wealth or power has done so by ignoring its coal and steel industries. This question is one not only of national but of empire importance. I do not know whether some hon. gentlemen opposite take much stock in that statement or not. Amid all this din and clatter and idle chatter about a new status being achieved, about Canada being at last a sovereign state, about our having wrested, as it were, a Magna Charta of Canadian liberties as if from some foreign and tyrannical power; amid all the signs and portents which indicate that this country is slowly and surely but blindly drifting towards independence from the motherland, there be those of us in this country who, yclept old-fashioned if you will, still think that there is something of value and virtue not only in strengthening the bonds that bind this great young nation to this great old empire, but in attempting also to foster and develop industries which are of empire importance. The Nova Scotia steel industry is an industry of that character. It is the only steel industry which has its roots in British soil, whose roots are indigenous to the British Empire. We have no other of the same nature in the empire. Should we not from empire considerations do what is fair, reasonable and just to see to it that this industry, so vitally important to Nova Scotia, to our nation, and to that great empire to which it is our priceless'privilege to belong, should not be allowed to deteriorate and to die?

who are ever willing to ridicule and to bring into disfavour constituted authority, and one: of the best ways in which to have constituted authority degraded, detested and despised is to have those who are responsible for enforcing that authority violate their plighted word to the people to whom they have given it. I say in all sincerity that my hon. friend has had a distinguished record both in peace and in war. For a number of years he has been a luminary of the Nova Scotia bar. He is a credit to himself and a Credit to the province whence he came. But the speech which he made on the budget, in which he dealt with the steel industry of Nova Scotia, was no credit to him.
